modules.title: Map barriers through a service journey
modules.outcome: Identify two interacting access barriers and propose an observable service requirement.
paragraphs: A digital service journey begins when someone first tries to find help. Map discovery, initial contact, completion, confirmation and follow-up. At every stage ask what the person needs and what the agency supplies. A successful web form measures only one point in the journey. People who give up while looking for the form may be absent from its records. [S71]

Consider device control, connection reliability, cost, language, time, physical access and support. A shared phone may be usable for browsing but unsuitable for a notification about a sensitive appointment. An intermittent connection can turn a twenty-minute application into repeated work. Describe each restriction in terms of the task it affects and avoid assuming that age or location can stand in for individual preferences. [R81]

Guo and Ogbodo studied experiences in six rural locations across Nigeria and China through focus groups with adults aged 50 or above. Participants raised different material and social barriers. Use the study to suggest what to investigate in a fictional pathway. The recruitment and specific sites limit how far the observations can be generalised, including to other Nigerian communities. [R81]

Turn the barrier into a requirement that a reviewer could observe. If a connection often drops at submission, a practical test could check whether someone can recover a short interrupted application without entering every field again. Also compare what the agency can collect through an assisted route and how the person receives a safe confirmation. State which claim the test supports and what you would still need to learn. [S76]
modules.example: Fictional case: A referral service uses a long online form and sends a detailed text confirmation. One person borrows a phone, another loses connection at submission and a third never finds the form.
modules.activity: Map the three different points of exclusion. Write two observable improvements and identify people missing from the form counts.
modules.feedback: Discovery, completion and follow-up each have separate barriers. Test recovery and a safe confirmation while keeping a staffed route available.

modules.title: Test accessibility in everyday tasks
modules.outcome: Apply keyboard, focus, error and authentication checks to a sample service flow.
paragraphs: Define a short end-to-end task, such as a person finding the referral form, choosing a safe contact channel, correcting an error and receiving confirmation. Record the version, device, assistive setup, expected behaviour and observed result. A blocker can exist after the home page, so run the task through the confirmation stage and include an unsuccessful attempt. [S72]

Use a keyboard to move through controls and confirm that the sequence follows the task. Observe whether the current control is visible, whether a banner covers it and whether buttons have understandable names when read aloud. A visible label helps everyone interpret a field, and the programmatically associated name helps an assistive device identify it. Test without assuming that one browser represents every setup. [S72]

When a person leaves a date blank, a clear error identifies the field, explains the next action and lets the person keep other answers wherever appropriate. Check that the explanation can be discovered through the keyboard and a screen reader. Authentication also needs attention. An accessible method can support a password manager or an equivalent option rather than requiring everyone to solve a memory puzzle. [S72]

Automated checks can flag certain patterns, while a human walkthrough can reveal confusing instructions, dead ends and burden across steps. Review whether contrast, zoom, narrow screen use and readable language let someone complete the whole task. A list of checks is a starting point. Explain the test coverage and remaining uncertainty, especially where involvement of disabled users and expert review would add evidence. [S76]
modules.example: Fictional case: A fixed banner covers the active field when a keyboard user tabs down. The form highlights an error in red without naming it, and login prevents a password manager from filling fields.
modules.activity: Describe one reproducible acceptance test for each problem. Include an expected result and one scope limit.
modules.feedback: Check focus visibility, a clear discoverable error and a usable authentication route. Record the version and environment for any retest.

modules.title: Design a staffed service alternative
modules.outcome: Specify an alternative route, handoff and monitoring plan for comparable access.
paragraphs: An assisted or in-person option needs a real decision purpose, an owner and enough time to act. A phone number without staffing or a callback commitment can create a second queue with a lower chance of reaching service. Compare the practical conditions and service outcomes of each route. Include hours, language support, privacy, transport and how urgent information is routed. [S71]

Ask how the person wants to be contacted, within the agency's safe options. Provide a choice the person can understand before committing to the route. If a contact may reveal the nature of the referral, agree on a neutral confirmation or another safe approach. Offer approved language and communication support without making a family member the default interpreter for confidential decisions. [S71]

An effective change preserves the person's place in the process when the route changes. Agree what the first worker can pass to the next, who acknowledges the handoff and how the person learns the next step. For example, someone who begins a request by phone should receive an accessible confirmation and know when the receiving team will respond. A route is only as usable as its weakest required step. [S71]

Start evaluation with a small classroom walkthrough using invented profiles. Compare who can start, complete and receive a timely response by route. Record reasons for abandoning or changing channel where the simulation supplies them. Volume and convenience may improve for one group while another loses access. Consider that a preference for face-to-face support may reflect trust and culture as well as material access, and use that insight when interpreting the exercise. [R81]
modules.example: Fictional case: A portal adds a help number, but nobody answers after midday and callers must make a new online account to keep their place. A confirmation message exposes the referral subject.
modules.activity: Design a staffed fallback. Define an acknowledgement time, safe confirmation and measures that compare routes.
modules.feedback: A usable fallback needs staff, continuity of place and a safe channel. Compare completion and response using similar service stages and disclose missing attempts.

modules.title: Map purpose and minimise collection
modules.outcome: Justify each fictional intake field and identify a privacy review decision.
paragraphs: Start a privacy review with the service action the person wants. An appointment request may require a safe return channel and rough availability. A later eligibility assessment may need different evidence. Document each purpose separately, including optional analytics or training. Grouping unrelated purposes under one vague label obscures what the agency actually intends to do. The Nigerian Act sets expectations for specified purposes, relevance, limits on retention and accountability. [S73]

Trace a field through collection, access, sharing, retention and disposal. Identify who decides why the field is collected and who processes it on an agency's behalf. A contractor's access to a document still needs a defined function and review. If the team cannot say how a field changes a legitimate action, challenge its collection and check whether an existing less intrusive value would suffice. [S74]

Removing obvious names may leave a record identifiable through a rare combination of dates, location and circumstances. Replacing a name with a case code protects certain workflows while someone with the key or enough context may still link records. Consider the recipient and realistic linkability when proposing a transfer. Use invented records for the exercise, and specify who can review the purpose and safeguards of a real transfer. [S73]

Plan decisions about correction and retention while designing the intake. Identify what triggers review, who can act, what exceptions may need assessment and how the request is communicated. A retention note needs an owner and an operational action beyond a line in a policy. Flag sensitive fields, novel processing and consequential decisions for the appropriate privacy review before a real service uses the proposed workflow. [S73]
modules.example: Fictional case: A booking form asks for a support date, a safe contact number, full case histories and optional research permission. Every staff member can open each record indefinitely.
modules.activity: Categorise fields by purpose and necessity. Draw their access, retention and correction routes.
modules.feedback: Separate booking from optional research. Challenge full histories, limit access by function and assign retention and correction responsibility.

modules.title: Explain meaningful consent and choice
modules.outcome: Separate service agreement, recording choice and a verified processing basis.
paragraphs: An agency needs to explain what service it offers, what information it uses and who can answer questions. Agreement to receive a service concerns the service relationship. Consent to record the conversation concerns a different action. A processing basis is the justification the responsible organisation identifies for a specific purpose under applicable law. The Act sets out multiple lawful bases, and organisations need to assess the applicable basis rather than relying on a general acceptance screen. [S73] [S74]

Consider what happens when a person declines an optional recording. A choice may lose practical meaning if the ordinary service becomes inaccessible or slower without explanation. Describe the purpose, alternatives, possible recipients and what continuing without the optional feature looks like. Check understanding in plain language. Record the decision contemporaneously and provide a way to change it through an accessible service route. [S71]

Where consent is the basis, the agency needs a way to demonstrate it. Under the Nigerian Act, silence and inactivity cannot provide consent, and the request needs a clear accessible format. Withdrawal affects future reliance on that consent and does not retrospectively invalidate processing already lawfully carried out. Determine treatment of existing records and other obligations with the designated lead, and tell the person what can be done and when. [S73]

Avoid seeking a blanket yes to future uses. A second use may require its own assessment, information and safeguards. For the exercise, keep a decision record with the purpose, version of the explanation, decision, date, available service alternative and responsible role. Escalate unclear situations, including significant power imbalance or uncertainty around legal authority, to supervision and privacy review. [S74]
modules.example: Fictional case: The team asks callers to agree to service, recording and later product development with one button. It treats silence as permission and has no manual appointment route.
modules.activity: Draft a plain-language recording choice and indicate who verifies the processing basis and manages withdrawal.
modules.feedback: Explain the specific use and an ordinary appointment option. Capture the choice and give an accessible way to revisit it.

modules.title: Protect work accounts and report incidents
modules.outcome: Choose protective account habits and route a fictional information concern.
paragraphs: A workplace account connects the practitioner to sensitive agency activity. Use named authorised accounts, suitably strong unique passwords stored through an approved manager and multifactor authentication where provided. Follow the agency's device and update procedures. A shared account makes actions harder to attribute and can leave former team members with access. Review barriers to using the approved method with the responsible support team. [S77]

A message asking for urgent access changes should be checked independently using an established agency contact route. Stop before opening unfamiliar attachments or sending information, and report the suspicious message through the workplace process. Follow the service desk's instructions for preserving evidence and handling affected equipment. Staff support and well-practised reporting can reduce delay when someone is uncertain how serious an event is. [S77]

When an unintended recipient receives a fictional case file, identify the information, action, time and affected channel without broadcasting the file further. Promptly tell the responsible incident and privacy teams. Follow their directions on containment, records and practical protection of recipients and affected people. Statutory breach assessment and notification depend on the facts and the controller's duties. The learner's role is prompt accurate escalation. [S73]

Access also needs a lifecycle. When someone moves from intake to another role, verify the new tasks and request that unnecessary permissions are removed through the approved process. A review can check that approved people can still do their work and that test or former staff accounts no longer have access. Use the documented continuity route when access is interrupted, and leave credentials out of support tickets. [S71]
modules.example: Fictional case: An invented team shares a login. A staff member receives an urgent request for a password reset through an unexpected channel and discovers a case attachment sent to the wrong inbox.
modules.activity: Identify three preventive controls and draft an incident note with the minimum useful facts and recipients.
modules.feedback: Use named accounts and approved authentication. Verify the request independently and report exposure promptly through designated routes.

modules.title: Distinguish digital tools and AI outputs
modules.outcome: Classify a digital feature by its function, inputs and evidence requirements.
paragraphs: A digital form can apply a written rule, a prediction system can estimate an outcome from past patterns, and a generative model can produce new text from prompts and context. A single interface can combine all three. Ask which function produced the output you see. Different functions have different evidence needs and specific ways to fail under ordinary service conditions. [S76]

A written rule can be traced to a criterion in an authorised policy. Its result is only as good as the rule, the data and the way the rule was translated into the form. A prediction needs a defined outcome, relevant test conditions and contextual interpretation. A probability alone cannot supply the facts of an individual case or establish authority to make a decision. [S75]

A text generator can produce fluent statements unsupported by its inputs. For any service-relevant claim, locate an original record or an authoritative current source and check whether it makes the same statement. Look for an invented source, a date placed in the wrong period and a claim that silently turns uncertainty into certainty. Keep unresolved claims out of a final factual record. [S75]

Use a paper exercise to compare three proposed features against the actual agency task. Record the intended input, what the feature creates, the evidence needed to check it and who has authority to decide. A reviewer must be able to understand the limits of the feature and decline it where the intended task can be delivered more safely by an existing staff process. Document that decision and its reasoning. [S71]

modules.activity: Classify the features and identify one way to verify each output before relying on it.
modules.feedback: Check the written requirement, the predictor in relevant cases and each generated factual claim against its source.

modules.title: Look for unequal errors and defaults
modules.outcome: Design a comparison that can reveal biased assumptions under specified conditions.
paragraphs: An error can be unevenly distributed even when a system appears accurate on average. A model may handle names in an expected format while repeatedly altering others, or treat a postcode as a stand-in for reliability. Examine who supplied the historical information, what the label represents and the effect that an error has on a person trying to access the service. [S75]

Construct a narrow comparison with fixed fictional inputs. Keep relevant evidence the same and vary one detail that should not determine the result, such as the layout of a name. Record the prompt or template version, expected result, actual output and error category. A comparison can expose a divergence in the exercise. An explanation of the mechanism or a wider fairness claim needs more evidence. [S75]

For service measures, make group sizes and missing records visible. Five errors in ten drafts and five errors in fifty drafts are different observed rates. The smaller sample carries greater uncertainty. Identify whether the assessment covers all relevant pathways and whether test cases were selected after seeing the output. Keep raw fictional counts alongside the rates, and avoid obtaining sensitive attributes simply to populate a dashboard. [S73]

Ask what happens when an individual disagrees. They need an accessible route for a human review, understandable reasons and a way to correct inaccurate information. Averages can hide practical barriers or serious rare errors. A fair review considers the severity and consequences of mistakes as well as how often they occur, then assigns responsibility for deciding whether testing is sufficient. [S71]
modules.example: Fictional case: Two otherwise comparable example referrals differ in spelling format. The generated summary turns one familiar spelling into a valid identity but suggests extra scrutiny for the other.
modules.activity: Define a paired test and document the expected outcome, possible error type and scope of the result.
modules.feedback: A divergence warrants checking model and workflow behaviour. Record the test version and limit the conclusion to the supplied evidence.

modules.title: Give reviewers real authority
modules.outcome: Define a human review role, stop conditions, escalation and a decision record.
paragraphs: Human oversight requires the reviewer to have evidence, time, competence and authority. A checkbox that confirms a long draft in seconds leaves little room to detect misleading claims. Give the reviewer access to the relevant source, a clear purpose, practical criteria and permission to return or reject the draft. Staff should know when to escalate beyond their own scope. [S75]

Define what calls for a pause in the exercise. Examples include a contradictory date, loss of a refusal, unsupported risk language and transmission outside the expected approved route. A severity threshold should describe what may happen to the person and what action follows. Create a fallback that can continue the service while a designated role checks the concern. [S71]

The Nigerian Act addresses solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects. Its provisions identify conditions and safeguards, including human intervention and ways to present a view or contest a decision. Before a real service relies on automation for consequential choices, refer the intended purpose and details to the responsible privacy and practice leads for an applicability and safeguards review. [S73]

Include the limits of the reviewer’s remit and the point at which responsibility passes to a supervisor. Record the reason for each consequential decision, the evidence used, the version of the workflow and the reviewer responsible. A second person can review disagreements where the agency process calls for it. A record of favourable outputs alone hides the work that oversight performs. Include examples of corrected and rejected outputs and use these findings to reassess staffing, training and whether the feature should continue. [R82]
modules.example: Fictional case: A service manager asks staff to confirm generated referral restrictions quickly. Workers cannot see the original record or send a draft back.
modules.activity: Specify two reviewer permissions, two stop triggers and the facts required to justify a final decision.
modules.feedback: Provide source access and authority to reject. Stop consequential unsupported claims and use the staffed review route.

modules.title: Preserve voice and source distinctions
modules.outcome: Separate a person’s account, worker observation, interpretation and agreed action.
paragraphs: Case documentation helps the person and the team understand what happened and what comes next. Record who supplied a factual claim, when the interaction occurred and what the person actually agreed to. Distinguish reported experiences from directly observed behaviour. The worker's interpretation belongs in a recognisable place and should identify its evidence and uncertainty. [S71]

Consider this invented source. The person says they could not take the call because other people were nearby. The worker observed that the person asked for a different time. Recasting that record as refusal of support changes the meaning and may affect future decisions. Preserve the stated privacy barrier, the preferred timing and responsibility for making contact. Include relevant observations without making a diagnostic inference. [R82]

A generated summary may compress disagreement, flatten emotion or replace local language with generic service labels. Ingram's baseline work identifies tensions about observation, presence and reflection. Most respondents had yet to use the tool with service users, which makes the findings useful for educational discussion about expectations. Treat the concerns as prompts for careful examination in your setting. [R82]

Read a fixed classroom draft against the original notes line by line. Mark whether each claim is supported, uncertain, absent or contradicted. Check whether a crucial preference or refusal was omitted. Then produce a short record with a dated source, appropriate attribution and the named role responsible for action. The actual date of the interaction and the date the note is written can be distinct. Label both explicitly when the distinction affects interpretation or later follow-up. [S75]
modules.example: Fictional case: The source records that a person requested a private time to call. The draft says the person was uncooperative, declined help and refused to explain the absence.
modules.activity: Write a revised four-line note separating reported account, observation, interpretation and next step.
modules.feedback: Record the person’s privacy reason and request. Attribute what was observed and mark any interpretation as provisional.

modules.title: Reconcile drafts before signing
modules.outcome: Detect additions, omissions, substitutions and misleading conclusions in a draft.
paragraphs: Begin with the intended audience and decision. An appointment update can be brief, while a formal case note may need provenance and enough context to review the action. Check names or fictional identifiers, dates, negation, who said what, uncertainty and agreed actions. Label an unsupported addition separately from a missing source detail. An altered detail can produce both types of error at once. [S75]

A fictional source might say an application arrived Thursday and the team has yet to confirm a meeting. A draft that says the team promised a meeting on Thursday combines an incorrect event with an omitted uncertainty. Correct the date's meaning and retain the outstanding decision. Do not infer that a neat chronological paragraph is reliable simply because all the dates sound plausible. [S75]

Reconciliation also checks how the text represents agency and relationships. A phrase such as refused service can conceal a limited choice about recording or timing. Restore the person's wording and agency where relevant. If a literal quotation is important, verify it with a reliable source rather than inventing quotation marks around a paraphrase. Seek clarification through the responsible route if the source contains conflicting accounts. [R82]

Include time to review, correct and sign when judging whether a documentation change is worthwhile. The Finnish social welfare pilot gathered facilitated workshop feedback and described perceived efficiencies, but it did not time documentation or use structured questionnaires. In a classroom comparison, note which error types people corrected and which would require a different workflow. A saved draft becomes a final record only after the defined review. [R84]
modules.example: Fictional case: The source lists an application received Thursday, a provisional meeting date and a refusal of recording. The draft announces a Thursday meeting and omits the recording choice.
modules.activity: Mark both changes and rewrite the action status and recording decision. Specify what a signer should verify.
modules.feedback: Thursday refers to receipt. Keep the meeting provisional and preserve the decision about recording before signing.

modules.title: Record consent and handle corrections
modules.outcome: Design traceable recording choices, review history and a correction route.
paragraphs: An approved recording workflow needs a specific purpose and an accessible explanation. Describe what would be captured, who can use it, how recording affects the meeting, how retention is handled and what happens if someone declines. For the classroom scenario, practise explaining a manual note option and checking that the person understands the choice before marking any recording decision. [S71]

Keep decisions about audio, a transcript, draft text and the final case record distinct. Different records serve different functions and may have different retention and access decisions. A real organisation assesses those conditions with its qualified lead. In the exercise, document source, draft version, review date and sign-off role without including real identifiers or copying a questionable draft into unrelated notes. [S73]

If an inaccuracy reaches the final record, record what was corrected, the reason, the authorised role and which subsequent uses may require review. Stop continuing use of the inaccurate version where the process allows and inform the responsible team. The agency process needs to handle the person's request to correct an account, retain required history and explain the outcome in a usable way. [S73]

Reflect on how digital recording affects attention. A worker may spend less time writing in the room, or focus too much on what the tool captures. The observed difference depends on task and context. In a simulation, compare a manual note and a reviewed assisted draft for the quality of the record, staff reflection and whether the person's own account remains recognisable. Allow time for the worker to consider what the record may have missed. [R82]
modules.example: Fictional case: The fictional team keeps audio, draft and signed note in one folder. A person later challenges a quote that caused an unnecessary referral restriction.
modules.activity: Propose a correction record, identify downstream recipients and give the person a clear response route.
modules.feedback: Assess the affected decision, track the correction and review recipients through the approved process. Maintain usable feedback and ownership.

modules.title: Define case states and accountable handoffs
modules.outcome: Specify state changes, accountable roles and a check for lost referrals.
paragraphs: Describe the real service action behind each proposed status. Received means information has arrived. Accepted means a receiving role has taken responsibility under its process. Scheduled means an appointment is agreed or assigned as specified. Closed needs a reason and an authorised decision. A label with different meanings across offices makes it hard to see who is accountable for the next stage. [S71]

Draw a line for each role from intake to follow-up. At the point where responsibility passes, show what minimum information moves, how the recipient acknowledges it and which worker handles a failure to acknowledge. The sender may need to follow up if a receiving queue is unavailable. Give the person a usable confirmation and avoid promising an outcome the service has yet to deliver. [S71]

Define what happens when there are duplicates, an incomplete referral or a case sent to the wrong team. A worker checks the source records and follows the authorised correction process. A role should be able to return an incomplete record with a reason and next action. Keep enough history to understand the decisions without replicating sensitive information into every handover channel. [S73]

Test the workflow using a small fictional timeline. At 09:00 intake sends a request, at 10:00 the team has not acknowledged it and at 11:00 it is found in the wrong queue. Walk through ownership at each point. Do the same for a confirmed referral and a request that needs clarification. Record observable outcomes that can be compared after a repair. [S76]
modules.example: Fictional case: The dashboard marks referrals complete as soon as intake sends them. The receiving team never acknowledges one request and the person receives a message implying a booked appointment.
modules.activity: Draw states with a trigger and responsible role for each. Add a timeout, follow-up and accurate confirmation.
modules.feedback: A send event belongs before acceptance. Provide accountable follow-up and match the message to the actual service status.

modules.title: Manage minimum access and version history
modules.outcome: Design task-based access, a correction history and an exception route.
paragraphs: Begin with tasks rather than broad job labels. The person scheduling a meeting needs the safe contact option and availability. A practitioner handling the case may need more context. A service evaluator may need grouped counts and definitions. Document actions each role must complete and which information makes them possible. Challenge convenience requests that expose case narratives beyond a defined function. [S73]

Separate view and change permissions in the workflow design. An intake worker may be authorised to create a request without editing a signed assessment later. A supervisor may approve reassignment while a service desk handles permission requests. Review exceptions through a named process with an expiry or reassessment point when relevant. In your classroom map, simulate who requests access and who reviews it. [S71]

Keep a reliable correction history for meaningful changes. For example, repairing a wrong appointment location should preserve when it was changed, who changed it and whether the person was updated. The new status needs to point staff to the current location. A history is useful where it answers an accountability question, and sensitive text should be limited to what that question requires. [S73]

Test the design using a paper permissions matrix and task cards. Ask whether each role can execute its ordinary tasks, whether a role can see more than required and how staff receive continuity support during an absence. Record one situations-based exception, the responsible approval role and how the exception ends. Revisit permissions when staff transfer or a workflow changes. Check permissions against the actual tasks again. [S71]
modules.example: Fictional case: An intake assistant can change signed assessments. A temporary covering worker has indefinite access and the calendar silently overwrites appointment locations.
modules.activity: Prepare a three-role access matrix and a correction record for the changed location.
modules.feedback: Limit permissions by function, review temporary access and preserve a dated correction with a safe notification.

modules.title: Plan outages and safe reconciliation
modules.outcome: Describe continuity, controlled recovery and indicators for follow-up failure.
paragraphs: Even a well-designed referral system can become unavailable. Decide how staff identify an outage, who coordinates the temporary route and which high-priority services require continuity first. Use the agency's approved fallback and arrange a safe response channel for the person. A continuity procedure helps practitioners explain what is known about delay and how the next update will arrive. [S71]

A fictional outage card can include a unique temporary reference, time, necessary information and the role responsible. Track whether the delayed request received a response and which service actions can safely wait. Give staff an approved way to check the latest outage instruction and agree a review time for requests that cannot wait. The procedure should avoid collecting more information merely because a usual validation step is unavailable. Any real temporary record uses the organisation's authorised storage and handling arrangements. [S73]

Reconciliation brings temporary records and actions into the restored workflow while identifying duplicate arrivals. Compare each temporary reference against the recovered queue and distinguish actions already taken from items still awaiting a response. Record who confirms reconciliation and how a mismatch is escalated. Do not assume that a restored login means every referral was accounted for. [S71]

Measure service continuity using examples of elapsed time, missed acknowledgement and unresolved mismatch. If eighteen of twenty fictional temporary cases reconcile, the remaining two need an owner and review. Record their state separately from the total instead of describing the exercise as complete. Rehearse the sequence and identify what would change after a different kind of interruption. [S76]
modules.example: Fictional case: Connectivity fails after two intake workers send forms. Twenty temporary records are created. The portal returns, eighteen records reconcile and two have uncertain follow-up.
modules.activity: Describe the temporary route and its return to the normal workflow. Assign responsibility for the unresolved cases.
modules.feedback: Trace every temporary reference against the restored queue. Keep the two unresolved records visible with assigned follow-up.

modules.title: Connect indicators to the service purpose
modules.outcome: Define process, outcome and balancing measures for a fictional digital service.
paragraphs: Begin with the decision the service is trying to improve. A referral team may want eligible requests to receive a timely human response. The number of templates opened measures activity. Referral acknowledgements within a defined period measure a service process. Whether people received useful support is an outcome requiring separate evidence. Define when the clock starts and stops before collecting a count. [S71]

Specify which records belong in the denominator. Suppose forty of fifty acknowledged referrals received a first response, and another twenty attempts were never acknowledged. Forty of fifty describes a later stage. Forty of seventy would describe a broader stage only if the seventy attempts are comparable and completely accounted for. Explain exclusions and use comparable denominators across periods. [S76]

Balance speed with quality, access and workload. In a fictional drafting trial, count the time to review and correct, whether material choices survived editing and how many records triggered escalation. Service users may value clarity and reduced repetition even when staff time is similar. Define what bad outcomes would warrant stopping and who checks for them. [S75]

The English FOI study describes reports of adoption by authorities. Read that as organisational behaviour in a defined setting. An organisation can adopt a tool and still have little evidence about accessibility, quality or outcomes. Use that difference to avoid interpreting dashboards of logins as successful service. Describe what new evidence would answer your actual outcome question and how to obtain it proportionately. An outcome indicator should reflect what people needed from the service. [R83]
modules.example: Fictional case: A service claims better access after template openings doubled. It reports 40 timely responses among 50 acknowledged referrals and ignores 20 earlier attempts without acknowledgement.
modules.activity: Define activity, timely response, missing attempts and two balancing measures. Give each measure a denominator or observation rule.
modules.feedback: Keep the stages distinct. Document the earlier lost attempts, review burden, and the quality and usability of the response.

modules.title: Compare options and explain uncertainty
modules.outcome: Interpret a fictional before-and-after comparison and propose a stronger design.
paragraphs: Decide whether the immediate question is feasibility, user experience, workflow performance or effect on outcomes. A small simulation can show whether staff can operate a prototype and find a named error. It cannot establish that a real service improved. A comparison under similar conditions can estimate differences on the chosen task, with caveats for the sample, timing, conditions and selection of cases. Capture departures from the task protocol. [S75]

Imagine a manual route with thirty timely outcomes among forty attempts and an assisted route with forty-eight among eighty. The counts rise, but the proportions are seventy-five and sixty percent. Compare definitions, complexity and staffing. If the new route started alongside longer opening hours and a new intake policy, a change in rates alone cannot isolate the effect of the drafting feature. [S76]

Try a stronger classroom comparison. Use the same task definitions for both routes, use predetermined sample cases, retain every outcome and ask reviewers to apply clear criteria. If the same worker completes both routes, changing the order across workers can reduce an obvious practice effect. Record when timing starts and stops and define how unresolved cases enter the results. [S75]

The Finnish pilot illustrates why a finding needs its method beside it. Facilitated workshop feedback can help identify usability problems and perceived benefits. The paper describes variation in use, with no structured survey or measured task times at that stage. A classroom plan can build on those questions while specifying consistent observation and capturing service-user experiences through an appropriately reviewed route. [R84]
modules.example: Fictional case: A manual route has 30 timely responses in 40 attempts. A new route has 48 in 80 after hours and eligibility changed. The report credits AI for the higher number.
modules.activity: Compute the rates and identify confounding changes. Propose a comparable fictional exercise with two predeclared measures.
modules.feedback: The rates fall from 75 to 60 percent. Define comparable tasks and account for concurrent changes before making an attribution claim.

modules.title: Monitor incidents and decide what changes
modules.outcome: Write a decision supported by defined measures, adverse findings and accountable review.
paragraphs: Draft a brief monitoring plan before a change begins. Describe the feature version, target task, acceptable performance and what would trigger review. Include an accessible way for staff and people using services to raise concerns. A manager needs an account of beneficial changes and possible harms before deciding whether to continue, modify or pause a feature. [S75]

Distinguish a near miss from a confirmed consequence. If a reviewer corrects a fabricated appointment before signing, the event still offers evidence about the workload and safety of the process. If a person relied on the wrong date, record the actual consequence and response. Use the agency's incident process in real service settings and keep details within the authorised route. [S71]

Summarise counts, denominators and what the test omitted. Check whether one group experienced more failures and whether the pattern is consistent across examples. A serious failure can deserve action even if only one case appears. Consider who participates in a review, who has authority to pause or restore an alternative and where disputed findings will be examined. [S75]

Make a decision that someone can test later. A fictional team might keep a manual route available and revise the draft feature before a follow-up comparison. Tell the receiving team and the people affected how to reach the temporary route. Record the unmet criterion, restoration condition, date and role that will decide whether the evidence is sufficient. Describe any effect on service access and staffing during the pause. Treat adaptation as a documented change to evaluate. [S71]
modules.example: Fictional case: A trial reports faster drafts. One generated record omitted a refusal that staff caught before sign-off. Another sent an incorrect date that a person relied on.
modules.activity: Classify the events, explain the review action and state a specific decision and return condition.
modules.feedback: Both events matter. Record the caught error and the actual consequence. Assign a reviewer and restore the affected route only after agreed checks.

questions.question: Which measure most directly captures a timely service process?

options.text: Total template openings.
Number of staff accounts created.
First responses within a defined period among eligible attempts.
Total characters generated.

questions.rationale: Measures should reflect the defined service step.

questions.question: What does 40 timely responses out of 50 acknowledged referrals describe?

options.text: 80 percent of all people needing the service.
40 percent of all residents.
A causal effect of AI.
80 percent among acknowledged referrals.

questions.rationale: The denominator determines the population the figure describes.

questions.question: What would complement a measure of draft production time?

options.text: Time to review, correct and approve a usable draft.
Number of draft title formats.
Page background size.
Total device purchases alone.

questions.rationale: Preparation and review together determine real work.

questions.question: What question can FOI adoption counts help answer?

options.text: How many people got better support.
How many responding authorities report using the technology.
What software caused better equity.
Whether a specific output is accurate.

questions.rationale: Reported adoption is a measure of organisational use.

questions.question: Which measure could reveal harm hidden by a speed gain?

options.text: Number of accounts with a profile photo.
Total folders created.
Material inaccuracies remaining at sign-off.
Number of headings exported.

questions.rationale: Balancing measures capture costs or harms elsewhere in the workflow.

questions.question: What can a paper simulation establish most directly?

options.text: The service's population effect over a year.
The prevalence of need across the region.
A universal outcome improvement.
Whether a defined team can execute the supplied workflow tasks.

questions.rationale: A simulation tests performance within its designed conditions.

questions.question: Which timely-response rates match the supplied counts?

options.text: 75 percent and 60 percent.
40 percent and 80 percent.
60 percent and 75 percent.
Both 75 percent.

questions.rationale: Divide the timely responses by all specified attempts in each period.

questions.question: Why does the comparison fail to isolate AI's effect?

options.text: Both rates contain percent signs.
Eligibility and opening hours changed in the same period.
The numerator increased.
The comparison used two periods.

questions.rationale: Other changes could explain part of the observed difference.

questions.question: How can the classroom comparison address practice from repeated tasks?

options.text: Always run one route second after coaching.
Exclude all corrections from timing.
Vary route order with comparable cases and common scoring criteria.
Change scoring after seeing the results.

questions.rationale: Task order can alter performance independently of the route.

questions.question: Which result fits a facilitated workshop pilot without measured task times?

options.text: A measured 30 percent saving.
A validated cutoff for all users.
A causal improvement in waiting time.
Reported experiences and issues to test further.

questions.rationale: The feedback method supports perceptions and design questions.

questions.question: What belongs in a plan for the fictional pilot?

options.text: Version, measure, stop trigger, reporting route and owner.
A promise that every benefit will appear quickly.
A dashboard with hidden definitions.
A fixed expectation that all drafts pass.

questions.rationale: A monitoring plan connects observations to decisions.

questions.question: Which event is a documentation near miss in this case?

options.text: The inaccurate date already used by a person.
An omitted refusal corrected before sign-off.
A successfully confirmed appointment.
A planned manual route walkthrough.

questions.rationale: The error was caught before it had the potential recorded consequence.

questions.question: Which response fits the incorrect date a person relied on?

options.text: Correct the dashboard only.
Ignore the event because average speed improved.
Restore accurate follow-up and route the incident through the authorised process.
Treat it as a formatting suggestion.

questions.rationale: Actual consequences require a service and accountability response.

questions.question: Why review a single consequential failure despite a low aggregate rate?

options.text: Counts are meaningless in every evaluation.
One event establishes the national rate.
It proves every future draft will fail.
Its impact may be serious and expose a preventable weakness.

questions.rationale: Frequency and consequences inform different parts of a decision.

questions.question: Which decision can a reviewer reassess later?

options.text: Pause the affected feature until a named owner verifies the date and refusal checks.
Make it faster at some stage.
Restart after enough time passes.
Move the incident log away from the team.

questions.rationale: Clear criteria and responsibility make a decision actionable.

courses.audience: Social work learners and practitioners developing digital practice skills through guided simulation.
courses.study_guidance: Work with supplied fictional records and fixed example outputs. Keep real client material, account credentials and audio out of coursework. Use the agency privacy and supervision route for decisions about real services. Try each activity before reading the feedback.
courses.practice_safety_note: Work with supplied fictional records and fixed example outputs. Keep real client material, account credentials and audio out of coursework. Use the agency privacy and supervision route for decisions about real services.
courses.outcome: Present a fictional service design with a safe fallback, evidence plan, decision authority and a reviewable continuation decision.

modules.title: Frame and compare service options
modules.outcome: Compare a human-led route and a bounded digital option using the same criteria.
paragraphs: Start with the fictional Northbank help desk and one service problem. Requests reach the desk but some are lost before receiving ownership. A service goal is that every eligible request is tracked to a timely response through an accessible route. State who is included in the measure, what failure looks like and what is outside the scope of the proposal. [S71]

Compare a manual route with a structured queue and a narrowly scoped assisted draft. Use common criteria for access, safety, staff effort, quality, feasibility and accountability. For example, a queue may improve ownership tracking while adding a device access requirement. A draft may help organise notes while introducing a need to check dates, recommendations and attributed statements. Include the resources and staff time each route requires. [S75]

Olawumi's IJSDS article discusses cultural fit, community relationships and language access in Nigeria through a narrative discussion. Use these themes to frame questions about the local pathway, such as whether proposed communication supports the person's preferred language and realistic service options. Do not import its unverified statistics or treat its recommendations as measured results. [S78]

Write one requirement that follows from an affected person's task, one from service delivery and one from governance. A requirement can take the form of an observable outcome, such as a person receiving a neutral confirmation that preserves place in the queue. Record the assumption behind each requirement and the evidence that would make you revise it. A well-defined problem can justify improving the ordinary route first. [S76]
modules.example: Fictional case: Northbank blames a lack of AI for missing referrals. It knows that requests sent after midday are unacknowledged but has yet to compare staffing, routes and queue responsibilities.
modules.activity: Write the service problem in one sentence. Compare two options against access, quality, privacy, effort and ownership.
modules.feedback: Start with the missing acknowledgement. Compare a staffed workflow and a bounded digital option under the same criteria.

modules.title: Rehearse exceptions and document safeguards
modules.outcome: Run a tabletop test of access, consent, errors, continuity and review responsibility.
paragraphs: Build a small set of fictional test cards: an internet interruption, an inaccessible field, a declined recording, a lost acknowledgement and a draft that changes the meaning of a case note. For each card define the initial state, expected safe response, responsible role and observable result. Include one ordinary case so the team can check that protective measures do not block the expected route. Use the same format for pass and fail observations so the team can compare them. [S72] [S75]

In the declined-recording card, let the person choose ordinary note taking and confirm what will proceed. The draft card can start with a request for a private callback. If the generated example changes this to a refusal of service, a reviewer should identify the discrepancy and preserve the correct action. Keep checks scoped to the supplied examples. [R82]

In the outage card, exercise the temporary reference, acknowledgement deadline and restored record reconciliation. Decide who will notice a mismatch and ensure that the person still has an access route. When mapping permissions and information movement, limit the data to the fictional task. A real service would need a responsible privacy review of purpose, sharing and safeguards. [S73]

Record planned and observed behaviour for each card. If a criterion fails, preserve the observation and assign a correction with a retest. The team can practise the manual route while the fictional design is revised. An accessible workflow needs real responsibility for exceptions, including a role that can pause the change and explain next steps to the person. [S71]
modules.example: Fictional case: The trial team has a single successful demo. Its test cards lack a lost connection, a refusal of recording and a draft that changes case meaning.
modules.activity: Write three exception cards with expected results, responsibility and follow-up if each test fails.
modules.feedback: The alternative route, review correction and accountable recovery must be demonstrable. Record a failed criterion and retest it after revision.

modules.title: Present a bounded launch decision
modules.outcome: Present a decision memo with evidence, conditions, ownership and a review date.
paragraphs: Begin the memo with the immediate decision. In this practicum the available outcomes are to continue a classroom trial, revise the design or pause it and use the fictional manual route. Give a reason tied to the goal and the most consequential result. A clear pause can demonstrate sound judgement when a feature undermines confidentiality, access or the integrity of a record. [S75]

Report performance in terms the reader can verify. Give the counts of eligible attempts, timely responses and unresolved cases. Include the route and version for each measure. Describe which evidence comes from the supplied simulation and what remained outside the test. A published adoption figure from England cannot answer whether Northbank's access or safety improved. [R83]

Explain what would be required before another decision. A proposed record review needs enough staff time to check meaning and an accessible correction route. A feasibility result can identify skills to practise, such as checking local language terms or managing an outage. Include a named role for observing any new condition and a review date when the evidence will be reconsidered. [S71]

Use a short oral or written briefing to make the decision accessible to someone who did not take part. Explain the goal, the person affected, the most relevant outcome, remaining uncertainty and the next responsible step. Reflect on whether participation and professional judgement were strengthened through the design. Keep a dated record of the exercise and the follow-up idea. Include the version reviewed so later results can be compared against a known design. [S76]
modules.example: Fictional case: Northbank reports all 10 ordinary cases completed. Two interruption tests lost acknowledgement and one draft changed the meaning of a recorded choice. The team asks to expand.
modules.activity: Write a five-sentence decision memo with evidence, one stop criterion, two revision actions and a named recheck.
modules.feedback: A bounded revision or pause is justified. Report ordinary successes alongside the three exception failures and define retest criteria.

questions.question: Which outcome directly addresses the Northbank problem?

options.text: Deploy a generator this quarter.
Open more draft windows.
Eligible requests receive a traceable and timely response.
Increase character count per record.

questions.rationale: A service problem describes what people need to achieve.

questions.question: What makes an options comparison fair?

options.text: Count staff time for only one option.
Measure adoption for one route and equity for the other.
Pick the shortest proposal first.
Apply the same access, quality, effort and accountability criteria to both routes.

questions.rationale: Common criteria reveal the actual trade-offs.

questions.question: How can learners use the IJSDS discussion in this exercise?

options.text: Ask practical questions about language, culture and community roles.
Infer the number of Nigerian agencies using a tool.
Claim the article measured the intervention's effect.
Apply one community model to all communities.

questions.rationale: Contextual argument guides questions and requires local verification.

questions.question: Which requirement can be tested directly?

options.text: Improve innovation across the field.
A person who switches routes receives a neutral confirmation and keeps their place.
Increase enthusiasm about AI generally.
Guarantee satisfaction for everyone.

questions.rationale: Observable outcomes can be checked against a test scenario.

questions.question: What would prompt reconsideration of a portal-only option?

options.text: It uses a modern colour palette.
The team held a meeting.
People in the supplied scenarios cannot complete intake on the available devices.
The proposal has a short title.

questions.rationale: A disconfirming observation needs to relate to the stated requirement.

questions.question: Which test adds evidence beyond the normal demonstration?

options.text: Repeat the successful demo unchanged.
Show the product logo from another angle.
Count attendees.
A request loses connection before confirmation and recovers through the fallback.

questions.rationale: Exception cards exercise conditions that can disrupt service.

questions.question: What is an expected result on a declined-recording test card?

options.text: The person continues with the ordinary approved note process.
Intake automatically closes.
Staff create a separate unofficial recording.
The team removes any record of choice.

questions.rationale: The test shows how a feature refusal affects the service route.

questions.question: How should a reviewer handle a draft that makes a callback request sound like refusal of help?

options.text: Accept it because a model produced it.
Correct it against the source and track the next safe contact.
Preserve the wording as a verified fact.
Escalate the person as disengaged based on the draft.

questions.rationale: The reviewer is responsible for meaning and action.

questions.question: What should the outage test verify after login is restored?

options.text: Only that the login screen opens.
That no staff remember the delay.
Every temporary reference is matched or assigned for investigation.
A total displayed without case status.

questions.rationale: Reconciliation connects temporary work to recovered responsibility.

questions.question: What should follow a failed accessibility criterion?

options.text: Delete that test from the record.
Assume all future criteria pass.
Declare success after a discussion.
A documented correction with a named owner and retest.

questions.rationale: Preserved observations support accountable improvement.

questions.question: Which opening justifies a classroom pause?

options.text: Pause the proposed route because exception tests lost ownership and distorted a recorded choice.
Adopt the proposal because ten ordinary cases completed.
Defer the decision without giving an owner.
Claim the wider service is proven safe.

questions.rationale: A decision should reflect the most consequential evidence.

questions.question: What could be missed by reporting only the ten completed tasks?

options.text: The service's working name.
Failures involving interruption and record accuracy.
The presence of a slide title.
The calendar month alone.

questions.rationale: Normal tasks and exceptions answer different readiness questions.

questions.question: Which claim is supported by an authority adoption study?

options.text: Northbank improved its referral safety.
Every local service should use the same system.
Responding authorities reported using AI in specified ways.
Northbank's draft is accurate.

questions.rationale: Use adoption research to inform questions about implementation.

questions.question: Which continuation condition can be verified?

options.text: Everyone feels ready.
A supplier expects improvement.
Three weeks have passed without review.
The named owner confirms every outage card has a tracked acknowledgement and every disputed draft is reviewed.

questions.rationale: Clear ownership and measurable conditions support reassessment.

questions.question: What makes the final memo understandable beyond the design team?

options.text: State purpose, people affected, findings, uncertainty and next authorised action.
Use internal abbreviations without explanation.
List only the software components.
Omit the unresolved outcomes.

questions.rationale: A concise decision record should help an independent reader assess the next step.
